items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1960-08-02
items.q: 1922. 22. When I went to play second trumpet with Joe Oliver at Lincoln Garden in Chicago.

ctx.x: When did you leave New Orleans?

1922. 22. When I went to play second trumpet with Joe Oliver at Lincoln Garden in Chicago. See? How long did you play that? And he was on the other. He was scabbing at that time. But he was such a popular man in Chicago. And he sent for me to play trumpet. And I just had finished a funeral with the Tuxedo Brass Band with Celestan Lita. You know? And they took me to the station trying to tell me, don't go. Because Joe Oliver was scabbing, man. I said, what is scabbing? I don't know.
You didn't even know what it was?

items.title: Louis Armstrong: Jazz Casual Interview, 1964-07-10
items.q: That's what I mean, because you couldn't do, you couldn't tell Joe what to do. Yeah. He was the boss.

ctx.x: Now you spoke before about how they didn't have the drums. Baby Dodds just played Woodblocks. Uh, that daughter's baby was there.

Yeah. Yeah. They didn't need him nowhere. They didn't use drums at all, right? No drums at all at that time. They were scared it would throw the needle off. I see. Yeah. So we got back good. But the only thing I have about those early recordings is that you didn't get that lead much. That's what I mean, because you couldn't do, you couldn't tell Joe what to do. Yeah. He was the boss. Yeah. Now those breaks that you two took on there. Well, yeah. Well, I put notes to his lead, whatever he made. I just, we didn't…
Was it a different kind of excitement to play with this band coming up from New Orleans for you, for the inspiration? It was a big thing for me.

items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1962-09-19
items.q: And then when I got out, King Oliver taught me how to read music and everything.

ctx.x: Now, can you tell us, just how did you learn to blow that horn right now?

Well, I've always been a disciple to Joe Oliver, who was top man when I was a kid. And in the meantime, I used to go around the streets in a little quartet singing, and we'd pass the hat. And I don't know, there was celebration there around New Year's Eve, everybody shoot the big pistols and everything. And my mother kept on trying to hide my stepfather's pistol, but I found it. And I was shooting on Ramport Street, the big street in New Orleans, and the detective hugged me, and I cried like a little baby. But…
Now, Mr. Armstrong, around about 1930, I remember reading in the paper that you were dead.

items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1960-08-16
items.q: I guess before I joined Joe Oliver

ctx.x: You hear so much about the Roaring Twenties, I didn't live it. Could you tell me a little bit about it?

Well, I can tell you, uh, a little, a little far back than that. I'm sure you could. Well, but this is a little far back than that. I'll say first and, uh, I guess before I joined Joe Oliver, you know, I was in New Orleans during the days, uh, of, uh, dance bands, and, uh, I noticed, uh, there were such things at the club where the members would die, you know? Yeah. And the musicians that started this up in the twenties, all from New Orleans, uh, what do you call me? Yeah. So if a member died, and, uh, they lay…
Yeah, well, do you feel that it used to swing more in the good old days, or is that just talking and swinging right now?
